analysis.investment_thesis: Nazara fails both Magic Formula screens catastrophically — Earnings Yield of ~1.1% (EBIT ₹115 Cr / EV ₹10,046 Cr) and ROIC of ~2.5% are far below the 12% and 20% thresholds respectively. You are paying 100x EBITDA for a business whose EBIT has grown at only 4.7% CAGR over 9 years while net profit has actually shrunk.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 25.5% over 9 years shows genuine top-line scaling through acquisitions
71% gross margin reflects an IP/digital distribution model with strong unit economics at the product level
Minimal financial leverage (D/E 0.06) reduces near-term balance sheet risk despite heavy acquisition spend
key_risks: Massive gap between gross margin (71%) and operating margin (2%) signals acquisitions are consuming all economics — SG&A and integration costs destroy returns
Net profit declined from ₹75 Cr to ₹51 Cr in FY25 even as revenue grew ₹486 Cr — dilutive acquisitions at scale
FCF turned negative (−₹82 Cr, 2025) while investing outflows hit −₹1,139 Cr, funded entirely by dilutive equity raises (+₹805 Cr financing CF)
red_flags: Earnings Yield ~1.1% — one-tenth of the 12% Magic Formula minimum; massively overvalued by any earnings-based metric
Net profit CAGR of −2.7% over 9 years despite 25.5% revenue CAGR — scale is destroying value, not creating it
Other income (₹80 Cr) nearly equals net profit (₹51 Cr) — the operating business alone barely earns anything; remove investment income and operating economics are near zero
Total assets surged from ₹2,753 Cr to ₹4,260 Cr in one year, almost entirely from acquisitions — goodwill risk is substantial and untested
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula verdict is swift and unambiguous: Nazara scores near-zero on both screens. EBIT of ₹115 Cr against an Enterprise Value of ~₹10,046 Cr produces a 1.1% Earnings Yield — roughly one-tenth of the 12% minimum required. ROCE of 2.5% is similarly disqualifying; a business must earn well above its cost of capital to merit a premium, and Nazara earns far below it. The EV/EBITDA of 100.8x and trailing P/E of 133.6x confirm the market is pricing in a decade of flawless execution before a reasonable return is possible.

The structural problem is the acquisition treadmill. Gross margins of 71% look enticing until you realize that nine years of 25% revenue growth have compressed net profit CAGR to −2.7%. Every acquisition adds revenue but also adds overhead, amortization, and minority interests that eat the economics. FY25 investing outflows of ₹1,139 Cr required ₹805 Cr of fresh equity; free cash flow was −₹82 Cr. The balance sheet is clean only because shareholders keep funding the gap. Until Nazara demonstrates that its portfolio of IPs can generate sustained EBIT margins above 10% and ROIC above 15% organically — without constant capital injections — there is no Magic Formula case to be made here.
